newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hewlett-Packard in $1 bln Singapore wafer venture.
newsitem.headline: Hewlett-Packard in $1 bln Singapore wafer venture.

text.p: U.S. computer giant Hewlett-Packard (HP) joined state-owned Chartered Semiconductor Manufacturing (CSM) on Thursday to announce a Singapore factory to make the wafer circuits at the heart of modern electronics.

CSM president and chief executive officer Tan Bock Seng said the plant, which will etch the tiny circuitry needed to run computers on to silicon wafers before they are cut up into microchips, would cost more than US$1 billion.

"This new facility will have a manufacturing capacity of more than 30,000 eight-inch wafers per month," Tan told a new conference. He said the circuitry would be no more than 0.35 micron wide and could be reduced to 0.25 micron or smaller.
Construction of the plant would begin in September and be completed by 1999, he said. Production would start in mid-1999.
The plant will be built and run by a joint venture, Chartered Silicon Partners.

The venture will be majority-owned by CSM, part of state-owned conglomerate Singapore Technologies group, with HP and the Singapore's government agency Economic Development Board holding minority stakes.
Announcing the joint venture, Singapore Trade and Industry Minister Lee Yock Suan said the new plant was one of 10 Singapore wafer fabrication plants in operation or under development.

"Although sentiments about the semiconductor industry are less bullish today in view of the current electronics slowdown, we believe the fundamentals of the industry are strong, and would continue to welcome investments in the wafer fab industry," Lee said.
"Singapore can potentially double the current number of wafer fab plants," he said.
Tan said the plant would make Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) which would be tailored to the exact requirements of individual electronics companies.
"This joint venture is meant to service customers on a worldwide basis. HP obviously has a lot of capacity to take out of this partnership," Tan said.
The general manager of HP's integrated Circuit Business division, Alan Marty, said his company would treat the new plant as if it were one of its own internal fabrication plants.
"We will be running our full product line through there. HP is in the server and workstation and printer and calculator business and we will be running ASICs for all those," he said.
He said HP had joined the venture because it needed an ever greater supply of circuitry in Asia.
